item.title: Team Identification
item.description:
Team identification is the extent to which a fan feels a psychological connection to a team and views the team as an extension of their self-concept. A highly identified fan experiences the team's successes and failures as personal successes and failures; the team becomes part of "who they are."Operationally defined by Wann & Branscombe (1993) and measured via the Sport Spectator Identification Scale (SSIS).Important caveat: Lock & Heere (2017) argue this definition conflates two distinct constructs — see Contested Aspects below.The team identification literature nominally draws on Social Identity Theory (Tajfel & Turner, 1979): Individuals derive part of their self-concept from group memberships Group membership provides self-esteem through positive distinctiveness of the ingroup People are motivated to maintain positive social identity, leading to ingroup favoritism and outgroup derogation Also draws on BIRGing/CORFing research (Cialdini et al., 1976): Basking In Reflected Glory: associating with successful groups to enhance self-esteem Cutting Off Reflected Failure: distancing from unsuccessful groups to protect self-esteem High identification makes CORFing difficult — the highly identified cannot easily distance from a losing team However, Lock & Heere (2017) demonstrate that the literature has simultaneously drawn on Identity Theory (Stryker, 1968) without recognising that IT and SIT are fundamentally different frameworks:The SSIS and subsequent research have mixed these frameworks inconsistently, producing theoretical ambiguity.Team identification functions as a psychological bond: Cognitive: The fan categorizes themselves as a member of the fan group; "we" language; team outcomes are personally relevant Affective: Emotional investment; joy at victories, distress at defeats; the team "matters" Evaluative: The team and fellow fans are viewed positively; outgroup (rival) fans viewed negatively Consequences of high identification (per Wann & Branscombe 1993): Greater behavioral involvement (attendance, following via media) Greater investment of time and money Self-serving attributional bias (success = internal, failure = external) Positive expectations maintained even after defeats Perception of team and fellow fans as "special" Social network alignment (friends are co-fans) Identification exists on a continuum from low to high, though some research treats it categorically (low/moderate/high). sources/wann-1993-ssis — introduced the Sport Spectator Identification Scale; foundational measurement paper Branscombe & Wann (1991) — early theoretical development linking team identification to SIT Tajfel & Turner (1979) — Social Identity Theory foundation Stryker (1968) — Identity Theory; largely unacknowledged in sport literature but implicitly drawn upon Cialdini et al. (1976) — BIRGing research establishing link between identification and self-esteem Heere & James (2007) — later extension examining team identity as nested within other social identities
sources/lock-heere-2017-identity-review — critical review exposing theoretical conflation; proposes fan identification vs. team identification distinction This is the most important critique in the team identification literature and should inform interpretation of all SSIS-based research.Lock & Heere (2017) demonstrate that the field has conflated two distinct theoretical frameworks: Identity Theory (IT) — Stryker's (1968) symbolic interactionist framework concerned with roles. People occupy multiple roles (parent, employee, fan) arranged in a salience hierarchy. Role salience depends on social commitment — the more one's social network is tied to a role, the more salient it becomes. "Being a fan" is a role one occupies and performs. Social Identity Theory (SIT) — Tajfel & Turner's (1979) cognitive framework concerned with group memberships. People derive self-concept from group belonging. Group identity becomes salient through situational cues and self-categorisation. Identifying with the team means seeing the team as a group of which one is a psychological member. These are not the same thing: A person might strongly occupy the role of "fan" (IT) without deeply incorporating the team into their social self (SIT) A person might feel deep group identification with the team (SIT) without structuring their social network around the fan role (IT) The mechanisms that make each salient are different (network commitment vs. situational cues) The self-esteem processes differ (role fulfillment vs. collective self-esteem) The SSIS conflates both: "How strongly do you see yourself as a fan?" — taps role identity (IT) Items about outcome importance — tap group identification (SIT) Items about friends seeing you as a fan — tap IT's commitment structure Items about behavioral displays — conflate identification with its manifestations Implications: We cannot interpret what SSIS scores actually mean theoretically Findings about "identification" may reflect group processes, role processes, or an unmeasured mix Different intervention strategies are implied by each framework, but we can't tell which matters 25+ years of research has predictive validity (SSIS predicts outcomes) but questionable construct validity (we don't know what it's measuring) Lock & Heere's proposed solution: Distinguish between: Fan identification (IT-based) — identifying with the role of being a fan Team identification (SIT-based) — identifying with the team as a social group This terminological distinction provides a path forward, though no new measures implementing it have been widely adopted. Unidimensionality vs. multidimensionality: SSIS treats identification as single factor. Some scholars argue identification has distinct cognitive, affective, and evaluative dimensions that should be measured separately. Relationship to behavior: Is identification a cause of fan behavior (attending, purchasing) or a consequence of it? Cross-sectional designs cannot establish direction. Attending games may build identification as much as identification drives attendance. Stability vs. malleability: Traditional measures assume identification is relatively stable. But can identification be deliberately cultivated? Reduced? The literature is largely silent on identification dynamics. Relationship to Giulianotti's taxonomy: The sport management tradition treats identification as a continuous variable measuring intensity. The sport sociology tradition (Giulianotti) treats spectator identity as categorical types with qualitative differences. These frameworks do not map onto each other cleanly.
concepts/birging-corfing — ego-enhancement/protection mechanisms enabled by identification; these phenomena are more consistent with SIT (group-based) but SSIS conflates them with role identity measures
concepts/spectator-taxonomy-giulianotti — alternative categorical framework; Giulianotti's "supporter" is characterized by "hot" identification, but the relationship between the frameworks is untheorized
concepts/psychological-continuum-model — the PCM provides the process account for how identification develops; high identification corresponds roughly to attachment/allegiance stages, but identification scales measure state while PCM describes movement
entities/ssis-scale — the dominant measurement instrument; subject to Lock & Heere's critique Psychological Commitment to Team (PCT) — alternative measure developed by Mahony et al.; does not resolve the IT/SIT conflation Fan Loyalty — related but distinct; loyalty implies behavioral persistence, identification implies psychological connection
Identification formation: The literature measures existing identification but says almost nothing about how identification develops. What causes someone to become highly identified? What are the pathways? This is the critical gap for fan origination research. Partial address: James (2001) provides the most direct evidence — children can form psychological commitment (the precursor to high identification) from age 5, with fathers as dominant socialising agent. The Psychological Continuum Model (Funk & James 2001) provides a process account — identification develops as fans move from attraction through attachment to allegiance — but does not empirically test stage transitions. Wann et al. (1996) provide exploratory data on origination factors. See concepts/childhood-origination, concepts/paternal-influence, and concepts/adult-origination. Identification change: Can identification be deliberately increased? Decreased? What causes identification to intensify or erode over time? Adult identification: Most samples are existing fans. How do adults who were not childhood fans develop identification? Cross-cultural validity: SSIS developed and validated in US context. Does team identification work the same way in collectivist cultures or different sport systems? Relationship to spectator taxonomy: No work integrates the team identification measure tradition with Giulianotti's categorical spectator types. IT vs. SIT separation: Lock & Heere (2017) propose the conceptual distinction but no widely-adopted measures implement it. We don't know whether role-based and group-based identification predict different outcomes or respond to different interventions. Team identification is the core construct for understanding why some fans are more valuable than others. High identifiers attend more, spend more, and remain loyal through losing seasons — they are the foundation of any fan base. But the identification literature provides no roadmap for creating high identifiers. It measures the outcome sports properties want but doesn't explain how to produce it.For Sporting Cultural Architecture, the Lock & Heere critique has direct strategic implications:If identification is primarily role-based (IT), interventions should focus on: Building social networks that commit people to the fan role Creating contexts where "being a fan" is a recognized, valued role with social investment The more social ties connected to the role, the more salient it becomes Implication: fan clubs, supporter groups, social events that embed the fan role in one's network If identification is primarily group-based (SIT), interventions should focus on: Making the team group psychologically salient Building collective self-esteem through shared category membership Intergroup dynamics (rivalry, distinctiveness) as mechanisms for strengthening identification Implication: emphasise "we," create ingroup markers, leverage rivalry These are different strategies. The current literature cannot tell us which matters more because it has conflated them. Any organisation serious about evidence-based fan development would benefit from testing whether role-commitment interventions or group-salience interventions are more effective.The Lock & Heere critique also suggests that measuring intervention effectiveness with SSIS is interpretively problematic. If scores change, we don't know whether group feelings, role commitment, or behavioral patterns changed.

item.title: Daniel Lock
item.description:
Daniel Lock is a sport management scholar known for critical theoretical work on identity and identification in sport fandom. Co-authored the influential methodological critique of team identification research with Bob Heere (2017). Lock & Heere (2017) "Identity crisis: A theoretical analysis of 'team identification' research" — the most significant methodological critique in the team identification literature, arguing that the field has conflated Social Identity Theory (group-based identification) with Identity Theory (role-based identification), producing 25+ years of theoretically ambiguous findings. Lock's work represents the self-critical turn in sport management research, questioning foundational constructs and measures that had been taken for granted. The Lock & Heere critique does not invalidate prior research but provides the conceptual vocabulary to recognise its interpretive limitations. concepts/team-identification

item.title: Identity crisis: A theoretical analysis of 'team identification' research
item.description:
The sport management literature has conflated two theoretically distinct constructs under the single label "team identification": social identity (group-based, rooted in Social Identity Theory) and role identity (role-based, rooted in Identity Theory). This conflation stems from the original SSIS development, which drew loosely on both frameworks without recognising their incompatibility. The field should distinguish between fan identification (role identity — identifying with the role of being a fan) and team identification (social identity — identifying with the team as a social group of which one is a member). Two distinct identity theories: Identity Theory (Stryker 1968) is rooted in symbolic interactionism and concerns roles within social structure; Social Identity Theory (Tajfel & Turner 1979) is rooted in cognitive psychology and concerns group memberships and intergroup relations. These are not interchangeable frameworks. (pp. 3-9) Different mechanisms for salience: In IT, role salience depends on social commitment (network ties to role-related others); in SIT, group salience depends on situational cues and cognitive accessibility. A role becomes salient through social structure; a group identity becomes salient through context. (pp. 8-9, 12-14) SSIS mixes both frameworks: Items like "How strongly do you see yourself as a fan?" tap role identity; items like outcome importance tap group identification; items about social networks tap IT's commitment structure; items about behavior (display, following) conflate identification with its manifestations. (pp. 15-18) Content validity problem: Because SSIS items draw on both frameworks inconsistently, the scale lacks clear construct validity. It may measure something real, but what it measures is theoretically ambiguous. (pp. 17-18) Terminological solution proposed: Use "fan identification" for role-based identification (seeing oneself as occupying the role of fan) and "team identification" for group-based identification (seeing the team as part of one's social self). These are related but distinct constructs. (pp. 20-22) Role salience hierarchy matters: IT emphasises that individuals hold multiple roles arranged hierarchically; the more socially committed one is to a role (through network ties), the more salient it becomes. This has been largely ignored in sport research. (pp. 6-8) Collective self-esteem distinguishes group identity: When team membership provides collective self-esteem (pride in the group, reflected glory), this is group identification operating. When identifying as "a fan" provides personal meaning and role fulfillment, this is role identification operating. (pp. 10-12, 19-20) Theoretical review and conceptual analysis. No new empirical data. The paper systematically compares Identity Theory and Social Identity Theory, traces how the sport literature has used both, and applies this analysis to critique existing measures and propose terminological clarity.This is the most important methodological critique in the team identification literature. Its contributions: Names the problem: The field has conflated two distinct constructs for 25+ years. Every SSIS-based finding is interpretively ambiguous because the underlying construct is theoretically muddled. Provides theoretical repair: By explicating IT and SIT as distinct frameworks with different mechanisms (salience hierarchy vs. situational accessibility; social commitment vs. shared category membership), the paper provides the conceptual tools to untangle the conflation. Offers terminological precision: The fan/team identification distinction provides a path forward for future research to specify which construct they mean. Raises construct validity questions: Forces acknowledgment that SSIS may have predictive validity (it correlates with outcomes) without having construct validity (we don't know what it's actually measuring). Theoretical, not empirical: The paper argues the conflation exists but does not empirically demonstrate that separating the constructs would produce different findings. The proof of concept is left to future research. No measurement solution provided: The paper diagnoses the problem but does not offer a new scale that properly separates fan identification from team identification. Researchers are left knowing the SSIS is problematic but without a validated alternative. Uncertainty about practical difference: It's possible that for most fans, role identification and group identification co-occur and predict the same outcomes. The paper cannot establish whether the distinction matters empirically. Does not invalidate prior research: The paper is careful to note that SSIS-based research has produced useful findings. The problem is interpretive ambiguity, not necessarily invalid results. But this nuance may be lost — the paper could be read as discrediting decades of research. concepts/team-identification — the concept this paper fundamentally critiques; requires substantial update to Contested Aspects

item.title: Craig Gavin Hyatt
item.description:
Craig Gavin Hyatt is a sport management scholar based at Brock University (St. Catharines, Ontario, Canada). His research focuses on sport consumer behaviour, particularly the formation, maintenance, and dissolution of team-fan relationships. Fandom de-escalation research: The 2015 Journal of Sport Management paper "Using Identity Work Theory to Understand the De-escalation of Fandom" (with William M. Foster) provides the first systematic empirical examination of how and why highly identified fans sever their team relationships. This directly answers calls from Funk & James (2001) and Mullin et al. (2007) for research on "downward movement" in fandom. Identity work theory application: Imports identity work theory from organisational studies to explain fandom as ongoing accomplishment, not static identity. Key insight: non-fandom is also an actively maintained identity requiring continuous work. Franchise relocation research: Earlier work (Hyatt 2007) studied Hartford Whalers fans left behind after franchise relocation, documenting how team loss creates lasting trauma and affects future fandom possibilities. Team tradition development: With Foster, developed conceptual model for strategic development of "fan nations" through invented team traditions (European Sport Management Quarterly, 2008). sources/hyatt-foster-2015-deescalation-fandom — fandom de-escalation study
concepts/fandom-de-escalation
concepts/fandom-as-career (related — Hyatt & Foster provide exit mechanism for Crawford's career framework) Hyatt works within the sport management/consumer behaviour tradition rather than sport sociology. His approach is interpretive/qualitative, using long interviews to understand lived experience rather than quantitative measurement. This positions him methodologically between the measurement-focused tradition of Wann and the ethnographic tradition of Crawford.The de-escalation research is notable for treating former fans as a population worth studying — most fan research assumes stable or escalating identification and ignores exit entirely. Sample limitations: The de-escalation study relies on a predominantly white, male, well-educated Ontario sample. Whether de-escalation dynamics differ by gender, culture, or geography is unknown. NHL/hockey specificity: Much of Hyatt's work focuses on NHL hockey in Canada, where the sport has distinctive cultural significance and where specific events (2004-05 lockout, franchise relocations) shaped the research context. Retrospective methodology: Reliance on participants' memories of de-escalation processes that may have occurred years or decades earlier creates potential reconstruction bias.

item.title: Using Identity Work Theory to Understand the De-escalation of Fandom: A Study of Former Fans of National Hockey League Teams
item.description:
Fandom is not a static identity but an ongoing process requiring continuous "work" to maintain. When fans experience a misalignment between their values and those of the sport object, OR when practical barriers prevent them from engaging in fan practices, they may de-escalate from active fandom to non-fandom. Critically, non-fan identity also requires active maintenance — former fans must continuously enhance the cognitive/emotional conflict and embed practical impediments to sustain their exit. Two pathways to de-escalation: (1) Misalignment of fan values (cognitive/emotional conflict between fan's values and sport object's perceived values), OR (2) Barriers to fan practices (practical impediments preventing material enactment of fandom). These can operate independently or simultaneously. Seven empirical themes for exit: sport in general (3/23), hockey specifically (5/23), league-level issues (19/23), team-related (9/23), individual players (5/23), media (6/23), life circumstances (15/23). League-level issues dominated, with the 2004-05 NHL lockout cited by all ten participants who were fans entering that season. Non-fandom requires work: Former fans maintain their non-fan identity by (1) enhancing cognitive/emotional conflict (reinforcing why the sport object's values conflict with theirs) and (2) embedding practical impediments (filling time with activities that preclude fan practices). This is not passive disengagement but active identity work. Three age-based cohorts with distinct de-escalation narratives: younger fans (avg 30) emphasised the lockout, middle-aged (avg 49) were turned off by violence/culture, older (avg 61) cited league expansion destroying the intimacy of the Original Six era. Team success not a standalone factor: Only one participant cited losing as a standalone reason; several cited winning as a reason (attracted bandwagon fans, diluted authentic identity). This contradicts Wann et al. (1996)'s finding that success is a primary cessation factor. Reverse socialisation potential: Several participants speculated their children or grandchildren might pull them back into fandom — a potential mechanism for re-engagement not explored in prior literature. National team support persists: Many former NHL team fans still watch international competition (Olympics, World Juniors), where national identity and perceived authenticity (amateur values, no commercialism) align with their values even when league-level fandom has ended. Interpretive qualitative study using semi-structured interviews with 23 former NHL team fans (24 interviewed; one excluded for not meeting criteria). Sample: 20 men, 3 women, aged 18-67 (mean 43), predominantly white, well-educated Ontario residents. Interviews conducted May 2011 to February 2013, averaging 35 minutes. Data collection ended at theoretical saturation. Coding used constant comparison method with iterative codebook development.Inclusion criteria: Participants had to demonstrate prior attachment/allegiance-stage identification with a former favourite NHL team and currently consider themselves non-fans of any NHL team. First empirical study of fandom exit: Directly answers calls from Funk & James (2001) and Mullin et al. (2007) for research on "downward movement" and "dropouts" from the escalator/continuum models. Identity work theory application: Imports identity work theory from organisational studies to explain fandom as ongoing accomplishment. Being a fan (or non-fan) requires continuous effort — identities don't persist automatically. De-escalation model: Three-stage model (Maintaining Fandom → Disrupting Fandom → De-escalating) with parallel cognitive/emotional and material/practical tracks. Provides mechanistic account missing from prior descriptive work. Non-fandom as active identity: Key theoretical insight that non-fandom is not mere absence of fandom but a constructed identity requiring its own maintenance work. This has direct implications for re-engagement strategy. Multi-level exit causation: Demonstrates that team-fan bonds are nested within sport, hockey, and league contexts; disruption at any level can cascade to team-level de-escalation. Sample homogeneity: Predominantly white, male, well-educated Ontario residents. Gender and cultural differences in de-escalation may exist but are not captured. Retrospective accounts: Relied on participants' recollections of processes that may have occurred decades earlier. Memory reconstruction may distort actual experience. NHL/hockey specificity: The NHL has unique characteristics (fighting, lockouts, expansion into non-hockey markets) that may not generalise to other sports/leagues. The 2004-05 lockout was an extreme event. No longitudinal tracking: Could not observe de-escalation in real time or verify predictions about future re-engagement. Canadian context: NHL hockey has distinctive cultural significance in Canada; dynamics may differ in US or international contexts. Non-fan sample only: Did not compare with fans who experienced similar disruptions but maintained fandom — cannot isolate what distinguishes those who exit from those who repair. concepts/fandom-de-escalation — central concept developed by this paper

concepts/team-identification — demonstrates that high identification does not guarantee permanence; identification can de-escalate entirely This paper provides the most actionable framework for understanding lapsed fan recovery:Which fans are recoverable? Those whose exit was driven by practical impediments (life circumstances, lack of time, relocation) rather than value misalignment are more recoverable. If barriers are removed, fandom can resume. Those whose non-fan identity is weakly maintained (not actively enhancing conflict, not deeply embedding impediments) are more accessible. The finding that children/grandchildren might pull former fans back suggests reverse socialisation as a re-engagement mechanism — targeting families rather than individuals. Which fans are likely unrecoverable? Those with deep value misalignment (perceive sport/league/team as greedy, violent, inauthentic) require the sport object to change, not just marketing intervention. Those who have embedded strong practical impediments (new sports, new hobbies, new routines) have high switching costs back to fandom. What must change for re-engagement? The seven themes tell us what broke — league-level issues (lockouts, expansion, rule changes), team management (greed, disrespect), player behaviour, violence culture. Most of the top causes (19/23 league-level) are not team-controllable. This is sobering: teams may have limited power to recover fans alienated by league-wide factors.Strategic implication: Maintaining fans is far cheaper than recovering them. Once non-fan identity is established and actively maintained, reversal requires either (1) major changes to the sport object, (2) removal of embedded practical impediments, or (3) competing identity demands (e.g., parenting) that override non-fan identity work. Prevention (keeping fans in the "repairing" stage rather than letting them fully de-escalate) is the key insight for Sporting Cultural Architecture.

item.title: Garry Crawford
item.description:
Garry Crawford is a sociologist of sport and leisure based at the University of Salford (previously Sheffield Hallam University). His work spans sport fandom, video game cultures, and digital media, drawing on interactionist and cultural sociology traditions. Fandom as career: The 2003 Sociology paper "The Career of the Sport Supporter: The Case of the Manchester Storm" introduced the career framework for understanding sport fandom. Drawing on Chicago School sociology (Hughes, Becker, Goffman), Crawford argues fandom is a fluid, bi-directional trajectory rather than a fixed identity state. Critique of fan typologies: Crawford directly critiques authenticity-based typologies (including Giulianotti 2002) for treating supporter identities as fixed categorical types. The career framework dissolves the "real fan" question. Neo-tribal framing: Applies Maffesoli's neo-tribes concept to sport spectatorship, emphasising fluid, consumer-oriented, overlapping allegiances. Adult origination documentation: The Manchester Storm case study provides the most significant empirical evidence of adult fan acquisition pathways in the corpus. sources/crawford-2003-career-supporter — career of the sport supporter
concepts/fandom-as-career
concepts/adult-origination
concepts/fan-typologies Crawford bridges sport sociology and cultural studies. Unlike Giulianotti (structural-critical tradition) or Wann (social psychological measurement), Crawford uses interactionist methods — longitudinal fieldwork, participant observation, interviews — to understand how people become and remain fans across the life course. This methodological approach makes him unique in the fandom literature for addressing temporality directly.Crawford went on to publish Consuming Sport: Fans, Sport and Culture (2004), expanding the career framework and engaging with media fandom. Later work addresses video game cultures (Video Gamers, 2012) and digital sport consumption. Single case study dominance: The career framework rests primarily on one case study (Manchester Storm) of one non-traditional sport (UK ice hockey) with a specific supporter profile (adult-acquired, middle-class). Generalisability to established mass-market sports remains untested. Career stages not validated: The seven career stages are analytically proposed, not empirically derived or operationalised. No measurement instrument exists. Neo-tribal framing may overstate fluidity: The emphasis on consumer-oriented, temporary allegiances may underweight the genuine fixedness of identity-based fandom documented in social identity research.

item.title: Spectator Taxonomy (Giulianotti)
item.description:
A four-category typology of football spectator identities proposed by Richard Giulianotti (2002), based on two intersecting axes: traditional-consumer (the basis of investment in a club) and hot-cool (the intensity of identification and its centrality to self-formation). The four types are: Supporter (traditional/hot): Grounded, local, obligatory identification; club as totemic representation of community Follower (traditional/cool): Nested allegiances across multiple clubs; mediated but culturally grounded Fan (consumer/hot): Intense but market-mediated, non-reciprocal relationship with club/stars Flâneur (consumer/cool): Detached cosmopolitan consumer; switches allegiances; virtual relationships Draws on three theoretical streams: Taylor and Critcher's commodification thesis (1970s): Football spectators shifted from "members" to "customers" to "consumers" as clubs pursued middle-class audiences Bryan Turner's sociology of body marks (1999): Hot loyalty = thick solidarity, permanent, obligatory; cool = thin solidarity, transient, voluntary Benjamin/Baudelaire on the flâneur: The detached urban stroller who collects experiences without commitment Sits within the figurational/critical sociology tradition (Elias, Dunning) rather than the sport management/psychology tradition.The two axes create four quadrants: HOT | SUPPORTER | FAN (traditional/hot)| (consumer/hot) | TRADITIONAL ---------|--------- CONSUMER | FOLLOWER | FLÂNEUR (traditional/cool)| (consumer/cool) | COOL Traditional-consumer axis: Measures the basis of investment Traditional: Local, cultural, historical bonds; non-market relationships Consumer: Market-mediated relationships; identification through consumption Hot-cool axis: Measures intensity and permanence of identification Hot: Central to self-concept; thick solidarity; permanent; obligatory Cool: Peripheral to self; thin solidarity; transient; voluntary Movement between categories is possible as commodification intensifies. The structural trend is from top-left (supporter) toward bottom-right (flâneur). sources/giulianotti-2002-supporters-followers-fans-flaneurs — original statement of the taxonomy Taylor (1971a, 1971b) — prior analysis of "soccer consciousness" and working-class supporter culture Critcher (1979) — member/customer/consumer distinction applied to football Turner (1999) — hot/cool and thick/thin solidarity framework Empirical validity: The taxonomy is entirely theoretical. No studies have tested whether spectator populations actually cluster into these four types or whether individuals move between them as predicted.
Disciplinary isolation: Sport management scholars (Wann, Funk, James, Trail) have developed parallel but different typologies (e.g., psychological continuum model, motivation scales) with no integration between traditions. Marketing scholars (Hunt, Bristol & Bashaw 1999) developed an alternative five-type typology with different axes entirely — see concepts/fan-typologies for comparison. Typology proliferation: Stewart, Smith & Nicholson (2003) critiqued the proliferation of untested fan typologies in this period, arguing they created conceptual confusion without empirical grounding. Nostalgia for supporters: Critics might argue Giulianotti romanticises "traditional" supporters and treats commodification as uniformly corrosive, underestimating agency and new forms of authentic identification. Flâneur overreach: The flâneur concept imports heavy cultural theory baggage (Baudelaire, Benjamin, postmodernism) that may overclaim the novelty or distinctiveness of detached spectatorship.
Career critique (Crawford 2003): Crawford argues Giulianotti's taxonomy (like all typologies) treats supporter identities as fixed categorical types when they are actually fluid positions within an ongoing career. Individuals move through positions bi-directionally across the life course — what appears to be a "supporter" or "flâneur" at one moment may be a career stage, not a stable identity. This critique suggests typological classification may be fundamentally misconceived. See concepts/fandom-as-career.

A fan at PCM's allegiance stage might be a "supporter" (traditional) or a "fan" (consumer) in Giulianotti's terms — the PCM does not distinguish between these, which is its limitation. concepts/fandom-as-career — Crawford's (2003) alternative framework that treats supporter identities as career positions rather than categorical types. Crawford directly critiques Giulianotti's taxonomy for treating positions as fixed when they are actually fluid and bi-directional. No account of how individuals become one type or another — the taxonomy describes states, not pathways Does not address whether adult-origin fans can ever become supporters, or if that category is structurally closed Limited cross-cultural application — developed for UK/European football; may not translate to other contexts Does not engage with the gendered dimensions of these categories The taxonomy forces sports properties to be honest about which spectators they are actually cultivating. Most marketing implicitly targets fans/flâneurs (consumer axis) while using supporter rhetoric. The key strategic insight is Giulianotti's paradox: flâneurs are parasitic on supporters. Properties that successfully convert all spectators to consumers may destroy the atmosphere that attracted them.For fan development: if childhood socialisation produces supporters and adult conversion produces fans/flâneurs, then the question is whether adult pathways can ever produce supporter-level attachment — or whether properties must accept that new adult fans will always be in the right-hand quadrants. This has implications for how "authenticity" is constructed and whether it can be manufactured.

item.title: Fan Typologies
item.description:
Fan typologies are classification schemes that distinguish different types of sports spectators based on underlying dimensions such as motivation, identification intensity, mode of relationship to teams/clubs, or behavioural expression. Two major typologies exist in the literature: Giulianotti (2002): Four types — supporters, followers, fans, flâneurs — based on traditional-consumer and hot-cool axes Hunt, Bristol & Bashaw (1999): Five types — temporary, local, devoted, fanatical, dysfunctional — based on situational-enduring motivation and centrality to self-concept These typologies emerge from different disciplinary traditions and serve different purposes.Giulianotti draws on: Figurational sociology (Elias, Taylor, Critcher) Bryan Turner's hot-cool solidarity framework Critical theory on commodification and the flâneur (Benjamin, Baudelaire) Hunt et al. draw on: BIRGing/CORFing (Cialdini et al. 1976) Information processing and schema theory (Fiske & Taylor 1984) Self-concept and attachment theory (Belk 1988, Ball & Tasaki 1992) HOT | SUPPORTER | FAN (traditional/hot)| (consumer/hot) | TRADITIONAL ---------|--------- CONSUMER | FOLLOWER | FLÂNEUR (traditional/cool)| (consumer/cool) | COOL Traditional-consumer axis: Is the relationship market-mediated or culturally/communally grounded? Hot-cool axis: Is identification thick, permanent, and obligatory — or thin, transient, and voluntary? Key distinction: temporary and local fans have situational motivation (external triggers); devoted, fanatical, and dysfunctional fans have enduring motivation (internally anchored in self-concept).Critical difference: Giulianotti asks what kind of relationship fans have (market-mediated vs traditional, thick vs thin). Hunt et al. ask how central fandom is to self and how constrained by situation. These are orthogonal questions. A Giulianotti "supporter" and a Giulianotti "fan" might both be "devoted" in Hunt's scheme — but their relationships to the club are structurally different. sources/giulianotti-2002-supporters-followers-fans-flaneurs — four-type sociological taxonomy
sources/hunt-bristol-bashaw-1999-fan-typology — five-type marketing-oriented taxonomy
concepts/spectator-taxonomy-giulianotti — detailed concept page on Giulianotti's framework Proliferation critique: Stewart, Smith & Nicholson (2003) argued that the proliferation of fan typologies in the late 1990s–early 2000s lacked empirical grounding and created conceptual confusion. Each new typology added categories without integrating prior work or testing whether the types actually exist in spectator populations. Empirical vacuum: Neither Giulianotti nor Hunt et al. tested their typologies. Subsequent work has not systematically validated either. Incommensurability: The two typologies are difficult to reconcile because they use different dimensions. A synthesis would require specifying how traditional-consumer relates to situational-enduring, and how hot-cool relates to self-centrality. Cultural specificity: Giulianotti's types are shaped by UK/European football culture; Hunt et al.'s by US major league sports. Neither addresses cross-cultural applicability.
Career critique (Crawford 2003): Crawford argues that all typologies are fundamentally flawed because they treat supporter identities as fixed categorical types rather than fluid positions within an ongoing career. The "real fan" question implied by typological hierarchies is unanswerable and unproductive. The alternative: understand fandom as a career trajectory through which individuals move bi-directionally across the life course. See concepts/fandom-as-career.
concepts/team-identification — the sport management tradition's continuous measure of identification intensity; does not distinguish types but provides a scale
concepts/birging-corfing — Hunt et al. use BIRGing to explain temporary fans specifically
concepts/hypercommodification — Giulianotti's structural driver of movement toward flâneur identity
concepts/psychological-continuum-model — complementary process model; typologies describe what kind of fan someone is at a given moment, while the PCM describes how they got there and how to move them. The frameworks are not competing — use typologies for diagnosis, PCM for intervention strategy
concepts/fandom-as-career — Crawford's alternative to typological thinking; treats supporter identities as positions within a fluid, bi-directional career rather than fixed types. The career model dissolves the authenticity hierarchies implicit in typologies and focuses on temporal trajectory rather than categorical classification No integrated framework combining insights from both traditions No empirical validation of either typology's categories
No account of how fans move between types (either within a typology or across them) — though the concepts/psychological-continuum-model addresses this at the process level by describing stage transitions rather than type classifications No typology addresses origination — how people become fans in the first place — only describes existing fans Gendered dimensions unexamined in both Sports marketers tend to reach for Hunt et al. because it is segmentation-ready: each type maps to tactics. But this accessibility comes at a cost. The typology obscures the structural and cultural dimensions that Giulianotti foregrounds.For Sporting Cultural Architecture, the critical insight is what each typology reveals about the other's blind spots: Hunt et al.'s blind spot: Two fans can be equally "devoted" (self-concept-central, performance-independent) but have radically different relationships to the club — one grounded in community and tradition, the other mediated entirely by market. Treating them the same misses what makes supporter culture valuable and vulnerable. Giulianotti's blind spot: His typology does not segment by marketing value or tractability. Supporters may be the most authentic but least susceptible to activation campaigns; flâneurs are fickle but responsive to fashion. A mature fan development strategy requires both lenses: understand the structural position of different spectator types (Giulianotti), then design targeted interventions (Hunt et al.) — without collapsing the distinction between them.

item.title: The Career of the Sport Supporter: The Case of the Manchester Storm
item.description:
Sport fandom should be understood as a career — a fluid, bi-directional trajectory through which individuals move across their life course — rather than as a fixed identity state or categorical type. Drawing on the Chicago School tradition (Hughes, Becker, Goffman, Glaser & Strauss), Crawford argues that supporter identities are processual, socially constructed, and subject to change in both directions. This framing dissolves the problematic authenticity debates that pervade fan typologies and instead focuses attention on the temporal dynamics of how people enter, move through, persist in, regress within, or exit fandom. Career trajectory model: Proposes seven stages of supporter career — General Public → Interested → Engaged → Enthusiastic → Devoted → Professional → Apparatus — representing increasing centrality of sport to identity and social networks (p. 227-230) Bi-directional movement: Unlike escalator models, careers can move down as well as up. Supporters regress, lapse, and re-engage throughout the life course. The trajectory is neither linear nor necessarily progressive (p. 230-232) Critique of typologies: Authenticity-based fan typologies (including Giulianotti's) are fundamentally flawed because they treat supporter identities as fixed states rather than fluid positions within an ongoing career. The "real fan" question is unanswerable and unproductive (p. 221-224) Neo-tribal fluidity: Drawing on Maffesoli's neo-tribes concept, Crawford argues contemporary sport support is characterised by fluid, temporary, consumer-oriented attachments rather than fixed community membership. Supporters can hold multiple, overlapping allegiances (p. 224-227) Entry points vary: The Manchester Storm case demonstrates that adult entry into fandom is possible and common — many supporters entered at the Interested or Engaged level as adults through work colleagues, partners, or entertainment seeking, not childhood socialisation (p. 228-229) Apparatus category: The highest career stage — where sport involvement becomes one's occupation (journalists, academics, club employees). These individuals have different structural relationships to sport than other supporters (p. 230) Incorporation/Resistance critique: Rejects the Frankfurt School-derived framework that divides fans into "authentic resisters" and "passive dupes." Both poles are sociologically unhelpful; most supporters occupy complex, shifting positions (p. 222-224) Design: Mixed-method case study of Manchester Storm, a British Ice Hockey Superleague teamData: 41 semi-structured interviews with supporters Survey of 1,400+ supporters 3 years participant observation (1997-2000) Context: Ice hockey is a "new" sport in the UK, allowing study of adult fan acquisition without the confound of childhood socialisation. Manchester Storm was established 1995, folded 2002.Strengths: Longitudinal engagement, mixed methods, unique population (adult-acquired fans of non-traditional sport)Limitations: Single case study, single sport (ice hockey), single nation (UK). The "new sport" context may not generalise to established sports where childhood origination dominates. Sample self-selected through fan networks. Temporal dimension: Prior frameworks (Giulianotti, Hunt et al., even PCM) describe positions or stages but treat them statically. Crawford introduces genuine temporality — fandom unfolds across the life course and the same individual moves through multiple positions. Bi-directionality: The explicit theorisation of downward movement (regression, lapsing, disengagement) is rare in the literature. Most frameworks are implicitly one-directional (fans get more committed or stay the same). Career as bridge concept: The career framework connects childhood origination (early entry, slow progression) to adult origination (later entry, potentially rapid progression or stagnation) within a single theoretical vocabulary. Dissolution of authenticity debates: By framing positions as career stages rather than identity types, Crawford sidesteps the unproductive question of who is a "real" fan. Adult entry routes documented: Empirically demonstrates that adults enter fandom through work colleagues, partners, entertainment seeking, and community participation — not just childhood socialisation spillover. Single case, unusual context: Manchester Storm was a new team in a non-traditional sport. Findings may not transfer to established teams with multi-generational supporter bases. No longitudinal tracking: Despite the "career" framing, data is cross-sectional. Crawford infers careers from retrospective accounts and cross-sectional variation, not actual tracking of individuals over time. Career stages are analytical, not empirical: The seven stages are proposed conceptually, not derived from empirical clustering or validated through measurement. Neo-tribal framing may overstate fluidity: The Maffesoli-derived emphasis on fluid, temporary allegiances may underweight the genuine fixedness of identity-based fandom documented elsewhere (cf. James 2001 on childhood commitment). UK ice hockey is niche: The supporter base skews middle-class, educated, adult-acquired — not representative of mass-market football fandom. No engagement with PCM: Crawford does not cite Funk & James (2001) or engage with the Psychological Continuum Model, though the frameworks address similar questions from different traditions. concepts/fandom-as-career — the central concept developed in this paper

Re-engagement should acknowledge this history rather than treating lapsed fans as new prospects. The Applied Note should focus on understanding where supporters are in their career and what caused regression.Adult acquisition: The Manchester Storm case demonstrates that adults can enter at various career stages (not just Awareness). Sports properties targeting adult acquisition should identify the entry points (work, partners, entertainment, community) and design pathways from those points.Against typology segmentation: Crawford's critique suggests that marketing segmentation based on fan "types" is flawed. Supporters are not types; they are careers-in-progress. Segmentation should be based on career position and trajectory direction, not categorical identity.Lapsed fan interventions: The gap between Enthusiastic and Devoted is critical — this is where careers often stall or regress. Interventions should focus on facilitating the social network integration that characterises higher career stages.Multiple allegiances: The neo-tribal framing suggests supporters can hold multiple, non-exclusive allegiances. This challenges the assumption that sport fandom is zero-sum competition for loyalty.

item.title: non-western-fandom-formation
item.description:
The majority of sports fandom research is conducted with US, UK, and Western European samples. The processes by which fandom forms in non-Western contexts — different family structures, collectivist vs individualist cultures, state vs market sport systems, different media environments — remain underexplored. Generalisability of existing models is untested.Sports are globalising, but fan development strategies are built on Western research foundations. Understanding whether childhood socialisation, team identification, and community attachment work the same way in Asia, Africa, the Middle East, and Latin America is critical for any property with international ambitions. Current models may be culturally parochial. sources/james-2001-cognitive-development-team-loyalty — provides detailed US evidence on paternal dominance (50% father-same-team), two-parent household dynamics, and gender asymmetry in childhood socialisation. Explicitly highlights the limitation: findings are specific to US Midwest, 86% two-parent households, and may not transfer to other cultural or family contexts. The paternal dominance finding in particular raises the question: does father-child transmission hold in cultures with different family structures, gender role expectations, or collectivist orientations?
sources/wann-1996-origination-continuation-cessation — US undergraduate sample; acknowledges sample limitations but does not examine cross-cultural validity. item.title: The Role of Cognitive Development and Socialization in the Initial Development of Team Loyalty
item.description:
Children can form genuine psychological commitment to sports teams as young as age 5, but the development of team loyalty in childhood is fundamentally shaped by two factors: cognitive developmental stage (Piagetian) and socializing agents — with fathers serving as the dominant influence. Children at preoperational, transitional, and concrete operational stages can demonstrate psychological commitment (cognitive complexity, resistance to change, volition), but not the behavioral consistency that characterizes mature loyalty. Commitment from age 5: Children as young as 5 years old demonstrated psychological commitment to a favorite team that was resistant to change. This is the earliest documented evidence of team commitment in the literature (p. 255). Fathers as dominant socializing agent: 50% of children who had a favorite team shared their father's favorite team. By comparison: siblings 31%, mother 12%, friends 8% (p. 252). Fathers' influence operated through attending games together, watching on TV together, and talking about teams. Strong gender asymmetry: No girls in the preoperational group (ages 5–6) had a favorite sports team. Within transitional group, only 4 of 10 girls had a favorite team vs 9 of 10 boys (p. 248). Sports spectating appears to be perceived as a "male activity" by young children. Mothers invisible despite engagement: All mothers in the sample reported having a favorite team and talking to their children about it — but no children associated sports teams with their mothers (p. 254). Children said mothers "don't like sports" or are "not interested in sports" even when objectively untrue. Psychological commitment without behavioral consistency: Children could demonstrate commitment (complex reasons for liking a team, resistance to hypothetical changes, volitional choice) but not the behavioral consistency of mature fans (frequent attendance, regular viewing, etc.) due to developmental and resource constraints (p. 252). Transitional stage matters: The study introduces a "transitional" category between preoperational and concrete operational, capturing children who can recognize transformations but cannot yet explain them abstractly. 40% of the sample fell into this category (p. 245). Television reinforces, does not originate: TV was not a primary socializing agent introducing children to teams; rather, it reinforced attachments first established through fathers (p. 257–258). Qualitative interview study using Piagetian clinical observation technique. N=50 children: 25 aged 5–6, 25 aged 8–9. Convenience sample from one elementary school in a large Midwestern US city (no top-level professional teams, but new MLS team and college sports present). Assessed cognitive development via three conservation tasks (number, mass, volume). Assessed team loyalty via questions on psychological commitment (cognitive complexity, resistance to change, volition) and behavioral consistency (attendance, TV viewing, reading, talking, merchandise ownership). Parental survey provided corroborating data on parent engagement with sports.Sample: 50% male, 68% Caucasian, 86% two-parent households. Single interviewer (author). Interviews tape recorded and analyzed using Q.S.R. Nudist qualitative software. First developmental account of fan origination: This is the first study to use cognitive developmental theory to explain when and how children become capable of team loyalty. It establishes that the capacity for psychological commitment exists earlier than previously assumed. Establishes paternal dominance: Provides the first empirical evidence that fathers are the primary socializing agent for sports fandom in childhood — more influential than mothers, siblings, or peers combined. This has major implications for understanding how fandom is transmitted intergenerationally. Reveals gender stereotyping in sport socialization: Documents that sports spectating is perceived as male activity even by very young children, creating an asymmetry in fan origination that likely shapes the adult fan base. Psychological commitment precedes behavioral consistency: Demonstrates that loyalty develops psychologically before it manifests behaviorally — children form commitments before they have the autonomy or resources to act on them consistently. Introduces transitional cognitive stage: Methodologically innovative in recognizing that children do not jump discretely from preoperational to concrete operational thought, but transition through an intermediate phase. US sample bias: Single Midwestern city with no top-level professional sports team. Findings may not generalise to contexts with different sport cultures, different family structures, or different levels of professional sport availability. Heterosexual two-parent family bias: 86% of sample lived in dual-parent households. The study cannot speak to fan socialisation in single-parent families, same-sex parent families, or households where primary carers are grandparents or other relatives. The "father dominance" finding is structurally constrained by sample composition. Gender asymmetry unexplored: The finding that no preoperational girls had favorite teams is reported but not deeply theorised. The study does not examine whether this reflects differential socialisation, cultural stereotyping, or other factors. Small convenience sample: N=50 from one school limits generalisability. No racial/ethnic diversity analysis beyond noting differences. Cross-sectional design: Cannot track how loyalty actually develops over time. Infers developmental trajectory from age-group comparisons rather than longitudinal observation. US sport ecosystem specific: Children's favorite teams included NFL, MLB, NBA, MLS, and college teams — a distinctly American mix. Findings may not transfer to single-sport cultures or contexts where club football dominates. concepts/childhood-origination — this paper is the primary empirical source for the childhood pathway

concepts/team-identification — developmental account of how identification forms (complements Wann's measurement work)
concepts/psychological-continuum-model — supports PCM's claim that psychological connection (attachment) precedes behavioral manifestation
sources/wann-1996-origination-continuation-cessation — corroborates that family is primary origination factor; James provides the developmental mechanism
gaps/non-western-fandom-formation — the US-specific findings highlight the need for cross-cultural research This is the most actionable paper in the corpus for understanding childhood fan development. The practical implications are significant: Target fathers: If fathers are the dominant transmission vector for fandom, sports properties should design experiences and messaging that facilitate father-child shared fandom — not generic "family" programming that treats parents as interchangeable. Age 5 is not too early: Properties often target "youth" programmes at school-age children (7+). This research suggests that by age 5, children can already form meaningful team commitments. The socialisation window opens earlier than typically assumed. Address gender asymmetry proactively: The finding that no preoperational girls had favorite teams reflects a cultural pattern, not a biological limit. If properties want female fans, they must actively counter the perception that sports fandom is a male activity — and this must happen in early childhood, not later. Mothers are invisible but present: Mothers are engaged with sports but children don't perceive it. This suggests a cultural framing problem, not an absence of interest. Properties that want to activate mothers as socialising agents must make maternal sports engagement visible and normalised. Psychological commitment is the foundation: Children form commitments before they can act on them. The goal in childhood is building psychological connection (attachment, meaning, identity linkage) — behavioral consistency (attendance, merchandise, media consumption) will follow when autonomy and resources allow. This aligns with the PCM's emphasis on moving fans from attraction to attachment. The paper's limitations must inform application: these findings are specific to a US, two-parent, middle-class context. Strategies derived from them may not transfer to other cultural or family contexts, and the female fan socialisation pathway remains under-theorised.

item.title: Daniel L. Wann
item.description:
Daniel L. Wann is a social psychologist and professor at Murray State University (Kentucky, USA). He is the most prolific researcher on sport fan psychology, with particular focus on team identification, fan motivation, and the psychological benefits of sport fandom. Sport Spectator Identification Scale (SSIS): Co-developed with Nyla Branscombe (1993), the foundational measure of team identification that enabled quantitative research on fan psychology Sport Fan Motivation Scale (SFMS): Developed scale measuring why people become fans (eustress, self-esteem, escape, entertainment, economic, aesthetic, group affiliation, family) Team Identification-Social Psychological Health Model: Theorized that team identification provides psychological benefits (social connections, self-esteem) that contribute to well-being Extensive research on BIRGing/CORFing, fan aggression, and psychological consequences of fandom sources/wann-1993-ssis — SSIS development paper

item.title: An Exploratory Examination of the Factors Influencing the Origination, Continuation, and Cessation of Identification with Sports Teams
item.description:
The factors driving fan origination differ from those driving continuation. Family and peers dominate why people become fans; team success and player quality dominate why they stay fans. This is the first empirical study to directly address fan origination as a research question, distinguishing it from the larger body of work that measures identification without asking how it forms. Origination factors (why fans originally started following their team): (1) parents/family (12.4%), (2) liked the players (10.2%), (3-4) friends/peers and geographical reasons (9.8% each), (5) team success (7.9%) (p. 997, 999) Continuation factors (why fans currently follow their team): (1) team success (16.1%), (2) players (13.3%), (3) geography (9.7%), (4) friends/peers (8.7%), (5) parents/family (5.5%) (p. 997) Cessation factors (why fans stopped following a former favourite): (1) team no longer successful (11.8%), (2-3) time constraints and loss of players (6.3% each), (4) geography (5.9%), (5) friends/peers no longer followed (5.5%) (p. 1000) Key shift: Family is #1 for origination but drops to #5 for continuation; success is #5 for origination but rises to #1 for continuation (Table 1). Fans are acquired through social channels but retained through performance. Over 40 distinct reasons were listed for each of origination, continuation, and cessation — identification is multidetermined (p. 1000) The three lists were positively correlated (Spearman rho = .52–.78), indicating some consistency in the factors across phases (p. 997) No significant gender differences in identification levels or number of reasons reported (p. 996) Exploratory, cross-sectional survey. N=91 undergraduate psychology students (44 men, 47 women, mean age 24.3) at Murray State University, Kentucky. Participants completed the SSIS for a current favourite team and a former favourite team, then listed reasons (open-ended, up to 40 lines) for: (1) why they currently follow their team, (2) why they originally began following it, (3) why they stopped following their former favourite. Responses coded into categories; percentages reported. No inferential statistics on category frequencies. Self-reported, retrospective data.First empirical study to directly ask how fans become fans — the origination question. Prior work (including Wann's own SSIS research) measured existing identification and its consequences but did not address formation. The finding that origination and continuation factors differ is important: family transmission creates fans, but performance keeps them. This implies that fans acquired through childhood socialisation may be vulnerable if socialisation bonds weaken and performance doesn't compensate.The explicit attention to cessation — fans stopping being fans — is also unusual. Most research assumes fandom persists; this paper documents that fans can and do de-identify, primarily when performance declines and social bonds erode.This paper's methodological modesty is partly why the origination literature remained underdeveloped for so long: Small convenience sample: N=91 US undergraduates at one regional university. Not generalisable to professional sports, other age groups, non-US populations, or non-college contexts. Retrospective self-report: Participants reported remembered reasons for becoming fans, which may reflect post-hoc rationalisation rather than actual causal factors. Memory reconstructs. Cross-sectional design: Cannot establish causation or observe actual origination processes. The paper calls itself "exploratory" and explicitly requests longitudinal and experimental follow-up (p. 1001). No inferential statistics on category frequencies: Percentages reported but no tests of whether differences between categories are significant. No pathway distinction: Does not distinguish childhood vs. adult origination pathways or ask when fans became fans — only why. Mean age 24.3: These are young adults; their "origination" likely reflects childhood/adolescent processes, but this is not verified. The paper is directional, not definitive. It opens a question rather than answering it — and subsequent literature largely failed to follow up. concepts/childhood-origination — family/peer factors support the socialisation account of childhood fan formation

Family and peers create fans through socialisation; success and player quality retain them. This has two implications: Acquisition vs. retention require different strategies: Community programmes, family experiences, and peer-group targeting may be most effective for acquisition (especially of children). Performance marketing, player promotion, and winning may be most effective for retention. Vulnerability window: Fans acquired through family socialisation but not yet anchored by intrinsic attachment (in PCM terms: at attraction, not yet at attachment) are vulnerable to CORFing when performance declines. The shift from social-origin to performance-dependent continuation is a risk moment. The cessation data also matter: time constraints, loss of players, and erosion of peer bonds all drove disengagement. Properties that fail to maintain social infrastructure (community, peer connection) and that experience player turnover or decline should expect fan attrition — and the attrition will come from those whose attachment is still extrinsically anchored.Methodological note: this paper's modest findings and acknowledged limitations may explain why the origination question has remained understudied. Doing it properly requires longitudinal designs and larger samples than this exploratory study could provide.

item.title: The Psychological Continuum Model: A Conceptual Framework for Understanding an Individual's Psychological Connection to Sport
item.description:
An individual's psychological connection to a sport or team can be understood as movement along a vertical continuum through four stages — Awareness, Attraction, Attachment, and Allegiance — governed by the increasing complexity and strengthening of sport-related mental associations. This is a process model describing how connections form and deepen, not a typology of fan types. Awareness (Floor 1): Individual learns that sports/teams exist but has no favourite; driven by socialising agents (parents, peers, media); marks lowest end of continuum (p. 125-127) Attraction (Floor 2): Individual consciously selects a favourite sport/team based on hedonic motives (entertainment, escape, excitement) and situational factors (promotions, star player, winning); connection is not durable — can CORF away when situational factors change (p. 127-131) Attachment (Floor 3): Psychological connection crystallises; physical and psychological features take on intrinsic importance and meaning; linked to self-concept, values, and attitudes; more complex associative network develops (p. 132-134) Allegiance (Floor 4): Loyalty characterised by persistence over time, resistance to counter-persuasion, biased cognitive processing, and consistent behaviour; attitudes are internally stable and guide behaviour automatically (p. 134-138) The model is bi-directional: individuals can move down the continuum (de-escalate) or remain stationary at any level indefinitely (p. 141-142) Key transition mechanism: as fans move up, the source of motivation shifts from extrinsic (situational, social) to intrinsic (values, identity, meaning) (p. 122, Figure 1) The involvement construct (attraction, sign, centrality, risk facets) can operationalise differences between stages — attraction-level fans score high on attraction facet but low on centrality; allegiant fans score high on centrality (p. 130-131) Conceptual/theoretical paper. No empirical data collection. Integrates prior research on sport spectators and fans under one framework, drawing on Hierarchy of Effects theory, Transtheoretical Model (stages of change), attitude theory (persistence, resistance, accessibility), and involvement research. Distinguishes PCM from Escalator Model (Mullin et al. 2000) by emphasising psychological processes over behavioural segmentation.First comprehensive process model for understanding fan development in sport management literature. Synthesises fragmented prior research (identification, involvement, commitment, loyalty) into a unified framework. Critically distinguishes between attraction (not durable, situationally contingent) and attachment (intrinsically important, linked to self-concept) — a distinction obscured by simpler identification scales. Acknowledges bi-directional movement and stationary positioning, addressing gaps in escalator-style models. Conceptual only: No empirical validation at time of publication; transitions between stages not operationally defined Socialisation underspecified: Acknowledges childhood socialisation research (Kenyon, McPherson, Lewko & Greendorfer) but does not deeply integrate it; awareness stage treatment is thin Adult origination implicit: The model applies to both childhood and adult pathways but does not differentiate between them or explore whether stage transitions differ by origination pathway US sport management tradition: Limited engagement with sport sociology (no Giulianotti, no figurational tradition); does not address structural/cultural dimensions Individual-level focus: Treats fan development as individual psychological process; community and collective dimensions undertheorised concepts/psychological-continuum-model — dedicated concept page for the PCM
