sources/giulianotti-2002-supporters-followers-fans-flaneurs — Giulianotti describes types; PCM describes movement between states The PCM is the most directly actionable framework in this wiki for fan development strategy. Each stage implies different marketing interventions:The critical insight is that attraction-stage fans can CORF away when situational factors change (team loses, star leaves, alternative entertainment available). Properties often mistake attraction for attachment and are surprised when "fans" disappear. The strategic imperative is to move fans from attraction to attachment — from extrinsic to intrinsic motivation — before the situational triggers expire.Connection to Giulianotti: The PCM describes movement; Giulianotti describes types at a given moment. A fan at the attraction stage in PCM terms might be a "fan" or "flâneur" in Giulianotti's terms (consumer axis, market-mediated). A fan at allegiance might be a "supporter" (traditional axis, thick solidarity) — but not necessarily. The PCM does not distinguish between traditional and consumer modes of attachment; that's the PCM's blind spot and Giulianotti's contribution.For Sporting Cultural Architecture: The PCM provides the process framework; Giulianotti provides the structural critique. Use the PCM to design stage-appropriate interventions, but use Giulianotti to ask whether those interventions are producing supporters or consumers — and whether that matters for long-term sustainability.

item.title: BIRGing and CORFing
item.description:
BIRGing (Basking In Reflected Glory): The tendency to associate oneself with successful others (teams, groups, individuals) to enhance self-esteem. Manifests in use of "we" language after wins ("we won"), wearing team apparel after victories, publicly associating with winning teams.CORFing (Cutting Off Reflected Failure): The tendency to distance oneself from unsuccessful others to protect self-esteem. Manifests in use of "they" language after losses ("they lost"), reduced display of team affiliation after defeats, psychological distancing from losing teams.Both concepts originated in social psychology research by Cialdini et al. (1976).Rooted in self-esteem maintenance and impression management. People are motivated to maintain positive self-regard; associating with winners enhances self-image while association with losers threatens it. BIRGing and CORFing are strategies for managing the self-esteem implications of group outcomes.Connects to Social Identity Theory: if the team is part of one's social identity, team outcomes affect self-esteem directly. After team victories, fans are more likely to wear team apparel, use "we" language, and publicly claim fandom After defeats, weakly identified fans distance themselves; highly identified fans cannot easily CORF because the team is too central to their identity BIRGing/CORFing asymmetry: highly identified fans BIRG strongly but cannot CORF; lowly identified fans can do both The inability to CORF is what makes high identification psychologically costly — you cannot escape the pain of losses Cialdini et al. (1976) — original BIRGing research with college football fans sources/wann-1993-ssis — demonstrates highly identified fans show ego-protective attributions; inability to CORF
sources/hunt-bristol-bashaw-1999-fan-typology — uses BIRGing specifically to explain "temporary fans" who engage during success then disengage Snyder, Lassegard, & Ford (1986) — CORFing research Whether BIRGing/CORFing are conscious impression management strategies or automatic self-esteem regulation Whether these patterns are universal or culturally variable Relationship to identification: is inability to CORF a consequence of high identification, or part of its definition?
concepts/team-identification — BIRGing/CORFing are downstream consequences of identification level Self-serving attributions — related ego-protective mechanism Impression management — broader framework within which BIRGing/CORFing sit Little research on deliberate BIRGing as fan acquisition strategy (can you get people to BIRG their way into fandom?) Whether BIRGing with successful teams can be a pathway to genuine identification Cross-cultural validity of the phenomena BIRGing suggests that team success creates opportunities for fan acquisition — people want to associate with winners. But BIRGing alone does not create the deep identification that prevents CORFing. Properties that attract "bandwagon" fans via success may find those fans CORF away when performance declines. The strategic question is whether initial BIRGing can be converted into genuine identification before the losses come.

item.title: A Conceptual Approach to Classifying Sports Fans
item.description:
Sports fans can be classified into five types — temporary, local, devoted, fanatical, and dysfunctional — based on the source of their motivation (situational vs enduring) and the centrality of fandom to self-concept. Each type requires different marketing strategies. Temporary fans are time-bound; they engage during specific events (World Series chase, Jordan's career) then disengage; motivated primarily by BIRGing (p. 442-443) Local fans are geography-bound; they support teams because of local identification but disengage if they move away or the team relocates (p. 444) Devoted fans have broken time/place constraints; fandom is linked to self-concept and they remain loyal through losing seasons; "my team right or wrong" (p. 444-445) Fanatical fans are like devoted fans but exhibit extreme expressive behaviour (body paint, costumes, shrines) that is socially accepted as supportive (p. 446) Dysfunctional fans use fandom as their primary form of self-identification; their behaviour becomes antisocial, disruptive, or deviant — e.g. hooliganism (p. 446-447) The typology may be sequential: fans can progress from temporary → local → devoted → fanatical → dysfunctional (p. 451) Each type requires distinct marketing tactics: timing for temporary fans, community embeddedness for local fans, information provision for devoted fans, expressive merchandise for fanatical fans, demarketing for dysfunctional fans (p. 447-450) Entirely conceptual. No empirical data. Paper draws loosely on three theoretical streams: BIRGing/CORFing (Cialdini et al. 1976), information processing/schema theory (Fiske & Taylor 1984), and self-concept/attachment theory (Belk 1988, Ball & Tasaki 1992). Examples drawn from US major league sports (NFL, MLB, NBA).Provides the first explicitly marketing-oriented fan typology, offering segmentation strategies for each type. Introduces the situational-enduring motivation distinction and the idea that different fan types require different marketing approaches. Acknowledges that BIRGing only explains temporary fans, not the persistence of devoted fans through losing seasons. No empirical validation: The typology is entirely conceptual and has not been tested Theoretical thinness: Draws on BIRGing, schema theory, and self-concept but does not integrate them rigorously; theoretical grounding is eclectic rather than systematic Pathologises intense fandom: The "dysfunctional" category treats extreme identification as inherently deviant, conflating hooliganism with dedication No social or structural dimensions: Ignores class, culture, community, and the market forces transforming fandom — all of which Giulianotti (2002) foregrounds US-centric: All examples are from US major leagues; no engagement with global football or other sporting cultures Ignores socialisation: The paper acknowledges (p. 451) that socialisation may explain fan development but does not incorporate this into the typology No measurement: Unlike Wann's SSIS, no scale or instrument is proposed; categories are intuitive rather than operationalised concepts/fan-typologies — comparative concept page situating this typology alongside Giulianotti's
concepts/birging-corfing — Hunt et al. draw heavily on BIRGing to explain temporary fans
concepts/team-identification — the devoted/fanatical/dysfunctional categories map loosely onto high identification
sources/giulianotti-2002-supporters-followers-fans-flaneurs — contrasting sociological typology; more theoretically rigorous but also untested This typology gets used in sports marketing precisely because it is marketing-friendly: it segments fans by their value proposition and prescribes tactics for each segment. But its thinness is a limitation. It treats fandom as an individual psychological state without attending to the structural, cultural, and communal dimensions that shape it.The key insight for Sporting Cultural Architecture is what the typology omits: there is no equivalent to Giulianotti's traditional-consumer axis, so no way to distinguish between a devoted fan whose attachment is community-grounded and one whose attachment is market-mediated. Hunt et al. would classify both as "devoted" because both are self-concept-central and performance-independent — but they may respond very differently to commodification pressures. The typology is useful for segmentation but misleading for understanding what fandom is.The dysfunctional category also reveals a marketing bias: the only pathology recognised is behaviour that threatens other consumers' experience. There is no recognition that commodification itself might produce dysfunctional outcomes for fans (alienation, exploitation, authenticity erosion).

item.title: Richard Giulianotti
item.description:
Richard Giulianotti is a sociologist of sport based at Loughborough University (as of 2014). A major figure in the figurational/critical sociology of football tradition, with over 75 publications and 3,700+ citations. Spectator taxonomy (2002): Four ideal-type spectator identities (supporters, followers, fans, flâneurs) based on traditional-consumer and hot-cool axes Hypercommodification thesis: Football since late 1980s has entered qualitatively distinct phase of market intensification Normative critique of commodification: With Adrian Walsh, developed philosophical arguments against treating sport as mere commodity concepts/spectator-taxonomy-giulianotti
concepts/hypercommodification
sources/giulianotti-2002-supporters-followers-fans-flaneurs Works in the UK sport sociology tradition (figurational, post-structural, critical) alongside scholars like John Bale, Gary Armstrong, and building on earlier work by Ian Taylor and Chas Critcher. This tradition is largely separate from the North American sport management tradition (Wann, Funk, James, Trail) — different journals, different methods, different theoretical commitments. Work is primarily theoretical and qualitative; does not engage with quantitative team identification research UK/European football focus; limited cross-cultural scope Critical normative stance may overstate negative effects of commodification

item.title: Subcultural Capital
item.description:
A form of status currency within subcultures, accumulated through embodiment of subcultural knowledge, values, and practices. Developed by Sarah Thornton (1995) extending Bourdieu's (1984) concept of cultural capital.In football supporter subcultures, subcultural capital is acquired through demonstrations of authentic commitment — continued attendance during unsuccessful periods, embodiment of key values (dedication, vocal support), deep knowledge of club history and traditions.Bourdieu's field theory and capital forms (economic, cultural, social, symbolic). Thornton applied this to club cultures (music scenes), showing how "hipness" functions as a currency. Giulianotti applies it to football supporter subcultures.Within supporter subcultures: Subcultural capital accrues to those who attended through bad times, not just success "Post-Hornby fans" (those who arrived during football's 1990s boom) are accorded lower status Embodiment of values (dedication, knowledge of traditions, vocal support aesthetics) confers status Critically: subcultural capital cannot be acquired through market consumption alone — buying merchandise does not confer authenticity Status gradations exist within supporter communities based on perceived volumes of subcultural capital. Thornton (1995) Club Cultures — original development of concept Bourdieu (1984) Distinction — underlying capital theory sources/giulianotti-2002-supporters-followers-fans-flaneurs — applies concept to football supporters Whether subcultural capital is genuinely distinct from cultural capital or just a domain-specific form How subcultural capital interacts with economic capital (can money buy authenticity indirectly?) Whether "authentic" supporter norms are themselves constructed and policed in exclusionary ways
concepts/spectator-taxonomy-giulianotti — subcultural capital is specific to traditional (supporter/follower) identities; consumer identities authenticate through market means Fan authenticity, gatekeeping BIRGing/CORFing (sport management) — different framework for understanding fan status displays How subcultural capital is transmitted intergenerationally within supporter families Whether new entrants can ever accumulate sufficient subcultural capital to be accepted as "real" supporters Cross-cultural variation in what counts as subcultural capital Subcultural capital explains why market-based approaches to fan cultivation have limits. Properties can sell merchandise and experiences, but they cannot sell the thing that grants status within supporter subcultures — endured commitment through hard times, biographical depth, non-market attachment. This creates a paradox for new properties: they have no bad times through which fans can demonstrate loyalty, no history for fans to know. The question is whether subcultural capital can be cultivated from scratch or requires time that cannot be compressed.

item.title: Hypercommodification
item.description:
A term used by Giulianotti (2002) to describe the intensified commodification of football since the late 1980s, qualitatively distinct from earlier commodification processes. Where commodification is the gradual entry of market logic into an object or social practice, hypercommodification denotes a step-change in scale, sources, and effects.Sits within critical/Marxist analyses of sport, drawing on Lash and Urry's (1987, 1994) concept of "disorganized capitalism" — postindustrial, postmodern, post-Fordist, characterised by intensified flows across globalised terrain rather than organised chains within national boundaries.Hypercommodification is driven by new capital sources entering football post-1988: Satellite and pay-per-view television networks Internet and telecommunications corporations Transnational sports equipment manufacturers (Nike, Adidas, Reebok) Public relations companies Stock markets (sale of club equity) Effects include: Greater migration of elite labour (players as global commodities) Proliferation of continental/global competitions Astronomical rises in elite player salaries New media outlets and cultural encodings of football Rise of "superclubs" as transnational corporations (Manchester United, Real Madrid, Juventus) Declining power of national associations relative to TNCs and superclubs sources/giulianotti-2002-supporters-followers-fans-flaneurs — introduces the term in football context Lash & Urry (1987, 1994) — disorganized capitalism framework Walsh & Giulianotti (2001) — normative critique of sport commodification Whether "hypercommodification" is a distinct phase or simply more commodification requires empirical specification of thresholds The periodisation (post-1988) is UK-centric; other football cultures may have different timelines Whether commodification is uniformly negative for spectator experience is contested
concepts/spectator-taxonomy-giulianotti — hypercommodification drives movement from supporter toward flâneur identity Commodification (general concept) — hypercommodification is an intensification, not a different process The concept is asserted but not operationalised — how would one measure hypercommodification? Relationship to parallel processes in other sports and entertainment industries unexplored Does not address whether hypercommodification is reversible or what resistance looks like For Sporting Cultural Architecture, hypercommodification names the structural environment within which contemporary fan development operates. All new properties are born into this environment. The question is whether fan development strategies can create supporter-type identification despite market mediation, or whether hypercommodification forecloses certain attachment pathways.

item.title: Supporters, Followers, Fans, and Flaneurs: A Taxonomy of Spectator Identities in Football
item.description:
Football spectators can be classified into four ideal-type categories — supporters, followers, fans, and flâneurs — based on two intersecting axes: traditional-consumer (the basis of investment in a club) and hot-cool (the intensity of identification). The broad structural trend under hypercommodification is movement away from the supporter model (hot, traditional, local, grounded) toward the flâneur model (cool, consumer, cosmopolitan, virtual). Supporters (traditional/hot) have obligatory, permanent bonds to their local club rooted in community identity; the club is a totemic representation of place; switching allegiance is impossible (p. 10-11) Followers (traditional/cool) maintain "nested identities" across multiple clubs via media; allegiance is non-local but still culturally grounded in football's traditions and symbolic exchanges (p. 12-14) Fans (consumer/hot) have intense but market-mediated, non-reciprocal relationships with clubs and stars; identification is authenticated through consumption of merchandise and media (p. 14-16) Flâneurs (consumer/cool) are detached cosmopolitans who window-shop across clubs, switching allegiances based on success or fashion; their habitat is virtual/non-place; solidarity is thin and simulated (p. 17-18) The hot-cool axis derives from Bryan Turner's (1999) work on body marks: hot loyalty = thick solidarity, permanent, obligatory; cool = thin solidarity, transient, voluntary (p. 9) Football entered "hypercommodification" post-1988 via satellite TV, stock markets, internet, and TNCs — a qualitatively different transformation than earlier commodification (p. 6-7) Supporters and flâneurs are paradoxically interdependent: flâneurs are "parasitic on people who are not cosmopolitans... you could not exist if there were not people who sat still and created the places that you visit" (Walzer, cited p. 21) Theoretical/conceptual paper. No empirical data collection. Draws on prior sociological analyses by Taylor (1971a, 1971b) and Critcher (1979) on football commodification, and Bryan Turner (1999) on body culture and solidarity. Uses ideal-type methodology in the Weberian tradition.Provides the first systematic typology distinguishing different modes of spectator identification, moving beyond the simple supporter/consumer binary. Introduces spatial and affective dimensions (topophilia, hot-cool) alongside the market dimension. Makes explicit that "fan" and "supporter" are not synonyms but represent different relationships to clubs. Frames commodification as transforming not just economics but the very nature of identification. Entirely theoretical — no empirical testing of whether these categories map onto real spectator populations UK/European football focus; limited engagement with how the taxonomy applies cross-culturally (acknowledges this but doesn't address it) The flâneur category leans heavily on cultural theory (Benjamin, Baudrillard) that may overclaim the novelty of detached spectatorship Treats the supporter-to-flâneur shift as a structural trend but provides no evidence of actual movement between categories The claim that supporters view themselves as "members" is inherited from Taylor/Critcher without critical interrogation of whether this was ever accurate Does not engage with the sport management literature on team identification (Wann, Funk, James) — exists in a separate disciplinary silo concepts/spectator-taxonomy-giulianotti — the core concept developed in this paper
concepts/hypercommodification — the intensified commodification process Giulianotti identifies
concepts/topophilia — the "love of place" that characterises supporter relationships to grounds
concepts/subcultural-capital — referenced re: how supporters authenticate status within the subculture This taxonomy is foundational for Sporting Cultural Architecture thinking. It forces clarity about which spectators a property is trying to cultivate or reach. Most sports marketing implicitly targets fans or flâneurs (market-mediated, consumption-authenticated relationships) while rhetorically invoking supporter language. The paradox Giulianotti flags — that flâneurs depend on supporters to create the spectacle — implies that properties which successfully convert all spectators into consumers may destroy the atmosphere that attracted consumers in the first place. For fan origination specifically: the taxonomy suggests different pathways produce different spectator types. Childhood socialisation likely produces supporters; adult conversion via media likely produces followers or fans. This has implications for whether new fans can ever become "real" supporters, or whether that category is structurally closed to adult entrants.
